summary.text: An 82-year-old man with arterial hypertension and a resolved herpes zoster episode two years earlier was admitted to the emergency department with high fever, confusion and reduced responsiveness worsening over 24 hours. On admission he was somnolent, disoriented and unable to follow commands with reduced tone and reflexes and bilateral extensor plantar responses; leukocytosis and raised CRP were found.

Despite empirical piperacillin–tazobactam for a suspected urinary tract infection, his consciousness deteriorated within the next 24 hours to a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3, and he was transferred to the intensive care unit, where he required endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.

CSF showed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose and EBV-DNA by PCR, with other viral PCRs negative; anti-EBV IgM was positive and IgG negative. Autoimmune and paraneoplastic panels, cultures and whole-body CT were negative. MRI showed bilateral thalamic T2/FLAIR hyperintensities with restricted diffusion and no enhancement, and MRA showed normal vessel patency. Bilateral thalamic EBV encephalitis was diagnosed and alternative causes were excluded.

Intravenous aciclovir, high-dose methylprednisolone and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started with supportive therapy. A follow-up MRI at 10 days showed persistent lesions without new abnormalities. The patient remained comatose without neurological improvement and died of multi-organ failure on day 18 of hospitalisation.
